utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom, but also just outside assisting us. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Josse you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to deal with one intercept immediately if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would first like to remind Mr. Krajisnik as I do every morning that you're still bound, Mr. Krajisnik, by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Josse you would like to start with the intercept, I do understand. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask that this be played. Could copies be handed to the Bench?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think they are handed out already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik needs a copy in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We even have a few copies. Which one would you -- no. There are two -- no, there is one. Yes, I've got an intercept, 3rd of December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right and could I say I'm very grateful to my learned friends for the Prosecution who are going to play this because we've been unable to do so on our equipment this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "Head of household because he is. Real heads of households, not a single one of them is a scoundrel. They must be Serbs since they are so nice. Real Serbs, no other town is more Serbian than Niksic, there you go. Oh, no there is none like it in the world. None like it in the world. I knew it, as soon as it was Niksic. Are you all right? How is it going? It's fine. How was it up there? It was great, I was with Vance for an hour and 25 minutes. We didn't make it public. Yes. But it's -- it was fantastic. Really. Those Americans, they are different. These European shits are unbearable compared to them. Well, what do you think, what's going to happen? Well, all right. I'll tell you. He wanted something regarding Bosnia and I refused, I told him first, please, tell this to the others in the European Community, when you come to Bosnia, if you don't see representatives of all three peoples and all three parties, you've seen nothing. Uh-huh. If you only see me and Izetbegovic, then again you've seen nothing. You must see the Croats as well. You must see all three sides. Hey, that's good. Otherwise you haven't seen you'll be misinformed. And second, no to the blue helmets. They say that the situation in Bosnia is difficult, well, it is difficult, but we are still maintaining the balance, there is no shooting. Uh-huh. If you come, that will disturb the balance and you will be the cause of unrest and clashes, and if you tell them that, it really bothers them when you tell them that they will be the cause. What do you mean, we will be the cause? All right. Since there is a lot of mistrust, the Serbs will think that the Muslims will manipulate you. The Muslims will think that the Serbs will manipulate you. Everyone will be tense and there will be disorder. You won't be able to bring the disorder under control because Bosnia is broad and there will be shooting and so on. It's best that you leave it alone. All right. Can we send unarmed observers? But would they be uniformed? Yes. Oh, well, I can't promise that. I have to see. You would deploy them in the Neretva River valley. I said, well, I can't decide about that on my own. I must ask my people. We are a democratic party and so on. But I think it's out of the question. Then he wanted the headquarters to be in Sarajevo. I said, Sarajevo is out of the question. Well, did he agree? No, he agreed. I said not in Sarajevo but it can be in Livno. He asked about Banja Luka, and I said, I'll let you know about Banja Luka because I was thinking, you know, if it has to be in Bosnia I suggested Ljubljana to him. Uh-huh. He said, there is no point because it would seem we were supporting Slovenia's secession. Uh-huh. He's strongly against recognition. Yes. Against recognition. I said, please we are not against recognition, but we are against recognition of unilateral acts. So, why don't we do it in the Federal Assembly, have Slovenia initiate the process of its recognition, and have Yugoslavia be the first country to recognise it? Uh-huh. And after Yugoslavia it can be recognised by everyone. And then use this experience for Croatia. He said we are afraid that the tension would increase because Croatia wants to be recognised and Bosnia also wants to; no, I said, Bosnia doesn't. And then I explained to him about our constitution and so on. He said, I read something about that. Did we send it to him? Did we? What? Uh, those documents of ours. Yes, we did. He said he read about it. Yes, we sent it, sent him a letter. A letter. And a reply came from him and he replied, did he? Yes, he replied. I'd like to see his reply. Nikola has it, I gave it to Nikola because he put my name on it and associates that with Nikola. Uh-huh. It was great. It was great. I sorted out many things with Slobo about his government and it's -- Listen, please. I'm listening. We have the constitutional committee session at 12.00 here, a Serbian one for the first time. Uh-huh. It would be good if you could come. Uh-huh. And at 1600 hours we have that, you know, our. Our? Well, I thought we could have a short one for about half an hour. To ask that Petko continue his work, you know, to continue work on our constitutional committee. Well, do I have to? Because I -- a foreign television crew is coming at 1300 hours. Well, if you don't have to, then don't. But I wanted to tell you I just thought it might be useful, it doesn't matter we will explain what it's all about. Our people are informed. I hope that the people from Krajina will come and the others who haven't. Oh, please one more thing. Yes. See if you can find, I need the Belgian political system and the Dutch political system. We should ask some of our people -- I don't know. I think someone had it. Lukic? I don't know who, the Belgian one is that right? We'll see now. The Belgian political system. Two communities living next to each other from beginning to end. Schooling authorities and everything is times two and then merges at the top of the state. Uh-huh. And there it merges on the basis of parity and with complete -- it's a very interesting situation. It would be good if it's true. I heard it from them and I received the Belgian ambassador here. He explained it to me, and there are enclaves and everything, you know, so that --. Well, there isn't. All right. In Holland, Protestant and Catholic children go to their own schools from beginning to end. All right. We have nothing against us living together. The only problem is that someone can't impose on others. The problem is manipulation and in position of will and if we can ensure that, everyone will breathe more easily when they see there is no imposition of someone's will. See here Radovan, please, this is what we agreed on here. I think it might be useful. We have the Main Board and the Deputies' Club sessions. They will last for a while because we have to decide on the economic -- then, you know, have the ministers submit and so on, we didn't want to be profane in the assembly. It's a disgrace when it's disorderly. It seems so common. It should all be prepared, decisions with invitations and everything and that it's official because on the 12th we also have -- All right. The Deputies Club here and in connection with the assembly, and that it be made official then because we should never put the assembly in a situation where it loses its dignity. All right, I agree, I agree. And there are no urgent decisions. It can all be done by the 12th and then if necessary adopt some decision on the 12th and we can prepare a bit, we have some material and so on. I think that the council sessions are on the 12th and we should decide tomorrow. I believe it will be a bit difficult for the one -- they will want to remove Begovic. We owe him a very big favour. Yes, yes. The way he is acting, and we also have to attack Doko. Yes, yes. And tomorrow, I don't know what the people want but I -- perhaps there should be a delegation now that we've begun, you know. Yes. But it's no good to walk out of the assembly. We must stay until the end and fight, you know. All right. We'll discuss it today and we'll see. But all right, then you'll come at 1600 hours and we'll have the club and the Main Board. Agreed. You know, so that it's at the same time. Agreed. So that we finish it. Agreed. We'll release you for 12 hours. All right, agreed. And you'll speak about what's going on there. All right. It will be a closed session so we can have a little talk. All right. Agreed. I'll inform the deputies and members of the Main Board. Agreed. All right."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note there is just one correction to make in the translation of the transcript. Would you like to hear that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes we would like to hear that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: After the word "Begovic," it should read, "we owe him a debt of gratitude," not "we owe him a favour."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction. No number has yet been assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D186, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D186. Mr. Registrar, if you would give me the copy, I'll -- I made the correction on the original so that it's -- and gave my -- I -- how do you say that, I put my initials with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Initialed it. Yes, we are grateful to Your Honour. Can I mention one logistical matter in this regard which I've discussed with the Registrar? And that's this. We would rather provide the audio CD of all the transcripts that we play at the conclusion of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there should be no problem. It should -- however, then perhaps you could, since you have to give a name to all of the files, the audio files on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should then reflect not only what you may have had in mind but also the numbers assigned to the exhibits by the Registry so that we -- for this one we find at least D186 as part of the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think that's technically not a major problem. We can give them the names we want, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure that's right. If there is any problem with it I'll revert to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll come back to us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note from the French booth. The French interpretation of the transcript hasn't finished so could there please be a pause? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have finished now and even the French booth has translated, the English booth pronounced that the French booth was not ready yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the beginning of this transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: At the beginning of this intercept, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Karadzic is clearly talking about negotiations that he has had with Mr. Vance?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Where did the negotiations that he is referring to take place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The media reported that this meeting was held in Belgrade, because Mr. Vance visited Mr. Milosevic and then he met with Mr. Karadzic as well. That's what this refers to, what Mr. Karadzic is saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is apparent from the detailed report that Mr. Karadzic is giving you, that you were not present at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic is clearly describing a negotiation that he had with someone in particular. Who was that person, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this pertains to the late Mr. Milosevic, when he was president. That's when the media reported that he met with Mr. Vance and his associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why were you not present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, I was a representative of the state, and I could not go to a meeting of this kind. How should I put it? Mr. Vance wanted to see the parties involved, the parties involved in Bosnia-Herzegovina were represented by the top people of the political parties, from Bosnia-Herzegovina there was Mr. Karadzic, who attended the meeting as the representative of the Serb party, the Serb side, and also the president of the Serb Democratic Party. So there was no possibility for me to attend in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On the first page in English, Mr. Karadzic talks about, I quote, "There is no shooting." What is that a reference to, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, also the late Mr. Vance came in order to reach an agreement with Serbia or rather with President Milosevic, to exercise his influence over the Serb Krajina, so that the UN forces could be brought in. Now, Mr. Karadzic is saying, in Bosnia there is no shooting, there is no war. Well, he didn't say like there is a war in Croatia, but it was necessary for the UN forces to go there. That's what he meant. Perhaps this was sporadic, but he said there is no shooting like in that other area, that is to say Croatia, which is why you, and he's referring to Mr. Vance, came, so that the blue helmets, the UN forces, would go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is the document that is being referred to a little later on in the conversation that you say you gave to Nikola because he put my name on it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably the letter that we sent or, rather, a letter, one of the letters that we sent. I can't remember now. One of the letters that we sent to the European Community, then, and to Mr. Vance. Since it was sent to me, but for Mr. Koljevic, then I forwarded it to him. I assume that that is the late Mr. Vance's response to what we had sent to him, a letter. I assume that it's that letter. I could not remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is then a reference to the constitutional committee, a Serbian one, for the first time. Tell the Chamber about that, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we established the Assembly of the Serb People in Bosnia-Herzegovina, like any assembly, it was supposed to have its commissions. Last time -- or, rather, I mean in Bosnia-Herzegovina the president of the constitutional commission was always the president of the assembly. Now, was this in accordance with some kind of document or was it just based on inertia, but that's the way it was. If you remember, we reached a decision to carry out preparations for adopting a declaration on the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Probably this commission had to meet in order to carry out these preparations. There was always a number of MPs involved and people from the outside. These were top legal experts who were there to interpret matters so that everything would properly be brought into a constitutional framework. So that's the constitutional commission. If you remember, Mr. Trbojevic came here, who was a member of the commission, both in Bosnia-Herzegovina when I was president and -- of the Serb republic, that is. And very often he kept taking my place. He had to take my place because I could not attend meetings. Excuse me. The president of the commission for constitutional affairs was supposed to attend various meetings. He stood in for me many times. So that's the constitutional commission of the Serb assembly in the Official Gazette we can even find the names of the members of that commission. I know that every MPs was a member of some commission and some MPs even served on two commissions because there were several commissions where MPs were supposed to be represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript uses -- says "Mr. Poplasen." That's clearly a mistake. The witness said "MP" and no doubt it will be changed in the correction process.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is then, Mr. Krajisnik, a reference to both the Belgian and the Dutch political systems by Mr. Karadzic. Why was he interested in the workings of those two countries?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that for the entire course of the talks, those two states, two legal systems, were an example for us. The Belgian and the Swiss one. Because they are all multi-ethnic states, entities and we wanted to apply their systems on Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina has some sort of roof authority, umbrella authority, and inside it there are different entities, units, like the Wallonians and the Flemish in Belgium. When we visited Belgium, we were told that there are Flemish and Wallonian neighbourhoods, and we thought we could -- within the same town, and we thought we could apply that to Sarajevo, organise it that way. I don't know to what extent such arguments were convincing but I know that Bosnia and Herzegovina were supposed to be transformed along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A little later on, you say, "the Deputies Club here, and in connection with the assembly, and that it be made official then because we should never put the assembly in a situation where it loses its dignity." What is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if this is true, this is the 3rd December and the assembly session was after the 11th of December, various agencies of the government, especially of the SDS on the municipal level and the republican level, wanted to attend the assembly session of the Serbian people. It was supposed to be a large gathering. And that would have virtually deprived the assembly of its autonomy. So I suggested to Mr. Karadzic to separate the preparatory meeting and have it held separately, the Deputies Club should meet separately, and have the assembly session without them so that it shouldn't turn into a fair. I was trying to keep the assembly more official, more ceremonial, because I thought a large number of outsiders would overwhelm it. I didn't want the MPs to be -- to be dominated over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Since the English transcript has been very helpfully corrected, let me ask you why you said that you owed Begovic a debt of gratitude?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Begovic was, I believe, deputy minister for National Defence. He was Mr. Doko's deputy, and he was a Muslim. But he was one of the staff who had been taken over from before, and he was advocating constitutionality in the domain of national defence in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he came into a conflict with the SDA because the SDA was favouring Doko, a Croat, rather than Mr. Begovic, who used to be an active-duty officer of the JNA, and I am saying, since the SDA wanted him replaced by somebody from their own ranks, who would be more amenable to the instructions of the party that appointed him, I said we owed him, meaning we, the Serbian side, owed him, because Mr. Begovic, a Muslim, worked for constitutionality and for giving the JNA the role that was due to it. If you remember, Mr. Kapetina testified here, and he explained all sorts of violations perpetrated vis-a-vis the JNA by the ministry. Mr. Begovic was very unbiased and objective in his work. That was my opinion. They later replaced him, but at this point in time, the situation was as I just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Begovic a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Just like Mr. Kapetina stayed in his position from the previous regime, Mr. Begovic stayed in the ministry and the SDA supported him, although he wasn't a member of the SDA. But he was a Muslim so he was automatically considered to be quote unquote, Muslim staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And presumably, the reason you go on to say that you have to attack Doko is for the reasons you have just given?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the reason I just named and for some other reasons I did not indicate. Mr. Doko did exactly as witness Kapetina explained in his testimony. He didn't recognise any laws, and he did a lot of things completely neglecting, bypassing the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Towards the end of the conversation, you say to Mr. Karadzic, "It's no good to walk out of the assembly. We must stay until the end and fight, you know." Explain to the Chamber what you meant by that comment, if you would, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking that members of the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian renewal movement, that is Serbian MPs, had already walked out of the parliament several times. When their constitution was being violated and their national interests were offended, they would walk out and leave me alone. I was saying that's not a good thing to do. We have to fight. We did put up our veto but we shouldn't walk out in anger. There were other walkouts by the HDZ and the SDB, and I would go and talk to them, trying to persuade them to come back. My idea was that just like we decided to participate in the work of the joint assembly and discuss only our own interests in the Serbian assembly, we should stay and fight for our rights in the joint assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for what we thought was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have no further questions on this intercept, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Just looking at one detail. When you said that you didn't want to make the assembly a fair, where too many outsiders would dominate, did you at that time have in mind the joint assembly still or were you at that time talking about the Serb assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the Serbian assembly, and I used a picturesque expression because that sort of thing did not happen in the joint assembly any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore I do understand that at a certain moment you're talking about the Serb assembly when you are discussing this, and at a later stage you're talking about how to operate in the joint assembly so as to defend yourself and not walk out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That we should not walk out of the joint assembly. You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Hanoteau also has a question. From the transcript it does not always clearly appear which assembly you're talking about but it's now clear to me. Judge Hanoteau?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In this Serbian assembly, how could external people who would attend the assembly -- how could they dominate the MPs? I don't really understand how that could be. What exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had 63 MPs. If we let in 50 members of the Main Board, seven or eight members of the Executive Board, maybe some people from the Regional Board, plus some other guests, then the MPs are outnumbered by non-members, and if I was talking about numbers, anybody present has the right to participate in the discussion, although MPs have priority. I was trying to say that this gathering would be 63 versus 80 non-members. That sort of thing didn't happen, but I wanted to prevent any such possibility. I didn't want the MPs to be overwhelmed by such a large audience and there was a keen interest on the outside in attending the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but is it constitutional or legal that guests to the assembly could actually take the floor and discuss and debate? Is that in the text? Is it provided for in the text? You know, to have people that are -- who are not MPs? That was in the text, that people who were not MPs could take part in the discussion, I guess they couldn't vote but they could debate? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Precisely. They were allowed to debate but they couldn't vote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have no other questions at this moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I take it Mr. Stewart has some further questions. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One or two, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, good morning. Mr. Krajisnik, we come -- chronologically we are really coming to January 1992. Just so that you can understand, Mr. Krajisnik, and feel comfortable about it but also to indicate to Their Honours and the Prosecution, there were two Serb assembly sessions held in January 1992, one was on the 9th of January, when a step was taken, the proclamation of the declaration of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then there was another session on the 26th of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, all that -- Your Honours, all that material is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm not going to ask you questions about those sessions. There may be method to my madness but just so you understand they haven't been forgotten; it's a deliberate decision not to ask questions at the moment about those sessions. The reason in a nutshell being that the points essentially get picked up later in subsequent sessions. So it isn't that January 1992 was a dead month, Mr. Krajisnik. But I do then want to go straight to something which indisputably happened at the end of January 1992 which is that you were in Belgrade, were you not, at the very end of that month?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in Belgrade. But I was never sure whether it was end December or the end of January, but I think you're right, it was the end of January, if we both mean one large meeting held in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, there is sufficient evidence that this event took place at the end of January that -- let's put it this way, I am not disputing it on your behalf in this Court. It's really clear that it was the end of January. You're referring to one large meeting held in Belgrade. Was Dr. Karadzic there as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what were you there for in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment ago I mentioned the visit of late Mr. Vance. The subject of our agreement was the bringing in of blue helmets to the Republic of Serbian Krajina, to areas that later became UNPAs. The leadership of Serbs from the Republic of Serbian Krajina, from this Croatian side of the Krajina, was opposed to the plan that later became -- came to be known as the Vance plan. The Presidency of Yugoslavia, headed by Mr. Kostic at the time, convened a large meeting, including representatives of the Serbian Krajina, Bosnian Krajina, four or five of us from Sarajevo, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, and myself, and there was also Mr. Mladic because he was at the time a commander of the JNA in Knin, and the purpose of that meeting was to exert pressure on the leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was then called SAO Krajina, to accept the Vance plan, and I believe we spent two or three days discussing from dusk until dawn to get them to accept that plan, and there were all sorts of representations made there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, we have -- Mr. Babic, of course, was a central figure in that particular event, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Late Mr. Babic was against it and, as you put it, he was the central figure, central figure to the opposition. He and his government were opposed to the plan, so they were the focus of the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what was the role of you, the Bosnian Serb group that you have mentioned, at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the president of Banja Luka municipality, people from Banja Luka region. We were a mixed group. It was not just the representatives of the Assembly of the Serbian People. Our role was to be used in order to exert pressure to get them to accept the Vance plan. When I say to be used, it's quote-unquote, of course, because we were supposed to participate, to contribute, to persuading the people from the Serbian autonomous district in Krajina who were closer to us and trusted us more, to accept the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you -- you said used quote-unquote. Was it your feeling that you were being properly used or that you were being exploited?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When somebody brings you in, in order to exert pressure on a third party in a matter that doesn't involve you directly, I cannot find a proper word for it. I don't think it was something bad. We were brought in to help exert that pressure. That's why I used that word, although it might have been better if I had said that we had been brought in to present our arguments and help persuade the SAO Krajina people. Until then, we didn't have any say. Nobody asked us anything. It was all between Serbia and the SAO Krajina. So I used the term conditionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there any significant differences of view in relation to that issue involving the Krajina and Mr. Babic, any significant differences of view among you, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It sounds a bit as if a cat is snoring or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A rather large cat, I think, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any source known for this? Are all microphones apart from mine closed at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I just closed mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seemed to help, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Maybe I was that cat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It wasn't me, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could be that construction works outside of this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French interpreter seems to think that it's because the panel, be that the microphone is against the panel and that's what's vibrating, from Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your microphone might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just moved it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It seems I was the source of the cat at the end. But maybe that will solve the whole problem. Seems to have done. My apologies. There it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik. Before that seismic interruption, I was asking you whether there was any significant differences of view in relation to the issue involving Krajina and Mr. Babic among you, Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And can you fairly briefly describe what those differences of view were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic, like Mr. Koljevic and I, were on the line that the Vance plan should be accepted, and we trusted the negotiators when they said that nothing -- no further improvements can be made, whereas Mrs. Plavsic sentimentally supported the leadership of the Serbian autonomous district of Krajina. She was saying that demands should be made for higher equality between the Serbian and the Croat side, so she differed in her opinion from us, the other side, including the Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did she keep those differences to herself in the more public meetings involving others than the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, she said that publicly at that meeting. She was even applauded for that by the Serbs, by the leadership of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina, as far as I can remember. Well it's not as far as I can remember, I'm practically sure that she said that publicly at this joint meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there, during your -- how long were you in Belgrade at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we worked all night, a day and a night, and that we even continued the next day. Perhaps it's two days and the whole night. We didn't even sleep. I don't know whether we went back home the next day or the day after that. I don't remember. But I know it was a long session, a day and a night and the following day. When the representatives of the Serb autonomous region did not come or the late Mr. Babic did not come to the meeting that was held the following day, there was just a short break. But we didn't sleep at all that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- during the whole time you were in Belgrade on that visit, did you, by which in this context I mean the Bosnian Serbs from Sarajevo, not including Mr. Babic in that, did you, the Bosnian Serbs from Sarajevo, have any discussions with anybody else about issues affecting Bosnia other than this particular issue about the Krajina and Mr. Babic and his colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is no because we were so preoccupied with the big problem. It would have been wrong for us to talk about Bosnia without having resolved the central issue at that meeting. All of the people who were from Belgrade left the meeting pretty soon, the following day, and the rest of us, we all went our respective ways. I think that's the way it was, as far as I can remember. If there was a meeting, these were unofficial meetings, but it's not that we discussed Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, at that time, you were in the -- still in the middle of negotiations under the auspices of the European Community, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. Well, yes, yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Portugal had taken over the Presidency as from the 1st of January 1992, for six months. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the answer is yes. Oh, yes, you're right, because Great Britain took over afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know at that time that you were going to be having an imminent meeting with Mr. Cutileiro?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, not at that meeting, though. I think that an initiative followed, primarily because the Muslim-Croat coalition had already passed a decision on the referendum and then the European Community got a bit more actively involved. I think so. I can't get the dates in the right order, it seems, but at any rate, around that time, the talks started and ambassador Cutileiro was there with his delegation, and he was a mediator, if I can put it that way, among the three sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll come to that quite soon, then, Mr. Krajisnik. Before we get there I want to ask you about a couple of other things. One is an exhibit which is P64A, binder 11, tab 264. I don't know whether Mr. Krajisnik gets that from another source. I have a copy for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may be premature. I was waiting for a copy for the Prosecution side as well but I see the usher is still involved in distributing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There seem to be two items on one little clip of paper, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Mr. Stewart. We just have a copy of the B/C/S so we are unable to follow this. We don't have all the binders with us, of course, and we did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not surprised. My apologies. I'll see if we can do something about that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from giving the exhibit number, could you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was going to just pause while Mr. Tieger gets the piece of paper. It's described 13th of February 1992 in the English. It's described as minutes of the meeting of the rather critically 00 Municipal Board. That's what we see and that seems to reflect the B/C/S as well from what I remember. But, Your Honour, it's not that item I'm going to ask about. It's the next one if we go on in the English two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you'll find a reference to -- you'll find the date the 17th of February 1992 and a heading, "Meeting of the Municipal Board of the Prijedor SDS." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that it's from Prijedor but I can't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It should be just above that. If you've got the meeting of the Municipal Board of the Prijedor SDS, the meeting was convened ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you see? It should have a date the 17th of February, just above that. Does it not, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see it. The 17th of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. And then agenda, about two or three lines under the heading, "Agenda. Report on the implementation of conclusions adopted at the meetings of the Main Board and the Serbian Assembly of BH after adopting the agenda. 28 members. Simo Miskovic, president of the" -- well, OO SDS we get again, "reported on the meeting held in Sarajevo." The key speaker was Mr. Karadzic, president of the SDS BH, the issue discussed was a BH act of secession carried out by the SDA. In view of this we are forced into the creation of national communities in ethnically defined areas. Then quotes, "The position of the European Community is said to have been that it would not interfere in internal arrangements in BH." Soon to follow is a debate on the constitution of a Serbian BH and then its adoption. The goal of the republic is to strengthen local authorities in the regions, economic and political, to the maximum. The region of Bosnian Krajina is also working in that direction. After the situation in the country has calmed down and proper conditions created, all Serbian territories and communities will be united by the will of the people. The international community has taken the view that it will not recognise a sovereign BH as an independent state. The SDA is largely engaged in sorting out the electoral rolls. Any participation by the Serbs in any form of referendum organised by the SDA is out of the question. In this context, it is necessary to put into motion the second level of the standpoint the main board of the SDS, BH. Party activists and commissioners must be sent to cover the entire territory and population (Serbs). Everyone should provide security, protection in their respective areas." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, can you -- can you say what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before we continue, I have on my screen, which should represent the exhibit as it was tendered, a different version of what seems to be the same document, but it may -- yes. Yes. The document that is in evidence has -- I wouldn't say a really different translation but it's at least another translation. Could we work on the basis of the documents that have been tendered? I'm now looking at P64 tab 264. It's not exactly the same, and I'm aware of the problem of double translations being made, but let's try to focus on what is in evidence in order to -- of course, if for one reason or another that translation would not be the best, we always could try to have it replaced for a better one but let's try not to work on the basis of so many different versions of the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I simply say I accept that. We do try. We will continue to try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We will probably from time to time fail simply because of the plethora of different versions of different documents but, Your Honour, we will do our very best to avoid this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I checked and P65 tab 89 seems to be also that different translation, and not the one you're using at this moment. So we find it in two sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not sure whether it makes me feel better or worse, Your Honour, that a different translation has been exhibited twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No. The only thing I'm trying to do is to make it clear on the record where we find the different versions of the same document, and neither of the two is the one you're using at this moment but I don't think that the differences are such. I'll follow on the basis of the other one and check whether there are such differences that it should be clarified or whether it's just a matter of words used, slight linguistic differences. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't dissent one iota from what Your Honour has said. The record also probably makes clear how difficult it is to cope with material in this way but we will do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- the bit that I just read, Your Honour, is that -- may I inquire, is that significantly different?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No it's approximately the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the specific key phrase, I think that is clear, was "it's necessary to put into motion the second level of the standpoint the Main Board of the SDS, BH." Can you say what was being referred to there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw that here several times. We heard that by way of testimony. I really don't know what this is. This is being tied to variants A and B but I cannot really bring that into connection with that provision because it seems that this is a consequence of the meeting that was discussed here through the bills from the Holiday Inn, as far as I can remember. So there was this joint meeting, negotiations were discussed, and it was already stated publicly that Serbia and Montenegro would be set up as Yugoslavia, as a core so to speak, so that it would be easier for Bosnia to be recognised and to go for ethnic units. That was the meaning. The interpretation was komisars but the word in B/C/S was "poveranici." Do you remember that in a way the positions of the president of the party were being transmitted. I'm trying to portray the situation as it is now but I cannot say with any degree of certainty what this second level is supposed to be. Perhaps the other variant. I don't know. Perhaps they thought along similar lines. Something like this. But I don't see how I can link this up to variants A and B. I don't know what they did. Prijedor did not do anything after that. You can see that through the documentation. I mean, through the documentation of the municipal board of Prijedor, you can see that before that and then and after that they did not do anything in connection with variants A and B. So I don't see what this would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, just for your information, there is a slight difference to the extent that the one translation is -- and that's the one -- let me just have a look. I think you used. No. The one you used talks about that it's necessary to put into motion the second level of the standpoint of the Main Board of the SDS, BH, party activists and commissioners, whereas the other speaks about the other translation says it absolutely necessary to cover the territory and the population (Serbs) by activists and representatives. So commissioners and representatives might not be exactly the same but that's the difference, the main difference, I identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I indicate how this happened? Because it may be of some help to others to avoid them chasing down blind alleys or something. I got the version I've got -- I'm not blaming anybody on the Prosecution side for this, Your Honour, but I got it from the footnote in the OTP pre-trial brief, which is, I suggest, not a particularly unreasonable thing to do sometimes when you're working but, of course, if the document which is footnoted in the OTP pre-trial brief all those years ago is a different version from the version has appeared in evidence, first of all it's not surprising this sort of thing happens and secondly why it might be helpful is just for Your Honours and others to realise that occasionally if one is working from that document, there is going to be a discrepancy between the footnoted document and the actual exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber has quite some understanding for the problems. At the same time, awareness of differences is I think most important to avoid whatever misunderstandings and confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. We are grateful to know that the exhibited version is different. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then a bit further down in this same document, well, immediately afterwards there is a heading, "Links with Serbia." Well, whether it's a heading or not, it says "links with Serbia." Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then several paragraphs and then a sentence, "We need to establish control over our territories. This has been agreed at the plenary session held before the queried joint session of the Serbian Assembly of BH in which Srdic as a deputy of the Serbian illegible of the Serbian people of Prijedor municipality took part." The reference to a plenary session there, Mr. Krajisnik, held before the assembly, what would you understand that to mean? It's a session of what or whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me where this is? I really can't find it. I saw the links with Serbia but I can't find this other part so that I see what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see some figures, 150 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1.5 million and it's immediately after that. It's the next line after the reference to 10 per cent of Muslims. It says, "We need to establish control over our territories. This has been agreed at the plenary session held before the queried joint end -- query session"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Here is a major difference in the translation, the other translation says preliminary meeting. Could we perhaps first -- Mr. Krajisnik, where a meeting is mentioned, is that a preliminary meeting in your language or is it a plenary meeting -- did you see, yes, a plenary meeting, Plenary Session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says pleminarni meeting here, pleminarni. That's what it says here, and that means a preceding meeting, a previous meeting. It says pleminarni here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, it can't say pleminarni in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note, yes, that is exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is not a Serbian word but that is exactly what the original says. It's a mistake in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's understood --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not right in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then at least it's -- it doesn't seem to be very much of a Plenary Session but rather a preceding or preliminary, but the language is unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, my apologies to the interpreters. It was a rather odd situation where a hybrid non-word in English was being produced as a translation from the Serbian. That was what was puzzling me, not surprisingly, perhaps. I'm still a little puzzled, to be frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krajisnik, whatever it's described as what sort of -- can you say what sort of meeting that was, of whom, that was held before the session of the Serbian assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting should be a broader meeting. Apart from the Club of Deputies, there were other participants before the Serb Assembly. This could be plenary meeting all throw that's not what is written here, so a bigger meeting the way I understand it before the meeting of the Serb assembly of B and H. That's what it says here. Where Srdic a Serb deputy from Prijedor took part. A Serb deputy of the Serb assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Serb assembly held immediately before this meeting here had been on the 15th, Saturday, the 15th of February. Leaving aside the text, do you actually remember whether there was such a meeting before the assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th of February. I do not remember. I just saw that there was a bill here from the Holiday Inn. I think it's the 15th of February. So that's how I think that there was a meeting, a broader meeting, before the assembly meeting. But I cannot remember now. If somebody were to ask me whether I remember, I don't remember, but I saw the bill and I believe that such a meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just -- it's about half a page on in the English, but do you see, then, Mr. Srdic speaks and then there is a reference to Mr. Miskovic and then a Dragan Sidjak speaks. Do you see that? Sidjak

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sidjak, Dragan Sidjak. The page is 534. If that is the text that reads, "He believe that is a Serbian BH," et cetera; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's exactly it, Mr. Krajisnik. My translation says he "believes that is a Serbian -- will only lead to war and does not think that the idea will work. He is convinced that a more realistic option would be a Krajina, particularly Sarajevo, as the centre. First of all, do you -- did you -- did you know Mr. Sidjak?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him once at a session but I did not talk to him. I know who he is but I didn't talk to him. I cannot say that I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When he refers there to a -- a Krajina, is it clear to you what he was -- what that Krajina would consist of?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have talked to the Trial Chamber here about a historical context, that there was an ongoing wish to unite the two Krajinas. This is not uniting the Serb Krajina and the Bosnian Krajina but generally speaking for the Autonomous Region of Krajina, well, I mean, that's what it's about, that Krajina, and he says that its capital would be Sarajevo and he says that that is a better option than having a Serb republic within Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what he's talking about, that it would be better for this region, this autonomous region, that already exists, that that should be some kind of separate entity and he did not mean uniting with the Serb Krajina, although on several occasions due to fear there was this idea which was prevented all the time and that is to unite the two Krajinas. Even as far as the Vance Plan was concerned that would have been a violation of the Vance Plan. We tried and we succeeded in preventing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then Mr. Srdic --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, perhaps I did not hear the right interpretation. He says, "in the Serb BH." But this is the recording clerk who is writing this, and it's as if he is saying it. He sees only war in the Serbian BH. I mean, he is not saying, I guarantee that there is going to be a war. His assessment is that there is going to be a war soon. So it is the recording clerk who was writing this down, so as if he said it. So he is conveying an opinion of his which is a bit different from him saying, "I think that" -- I mean it would be different if he called for war himself. He simply thinks that the situation is such that there is going to be a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There also is a slight difference in translation. Let me just check. The version you are using reads, "He believes that a Serbian BH will only lead to war and does not think that the idea will work." Whereas the other translation says, "He only sees war in the Serbian BH." Which is not exactly the same. And thinks that it could not function. Just to draw your attention to differences in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I was going to say I have one more question on this document so perhaps I can proceed with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Srdic who speaks then shortly very shortly after, there's Miskovic's response and Srdic, "we've seen that he is a deputy in the Serb Assembly." He says, "An important argument in our transformation is the plebiscite that we have held. The creation of states entails massive emigration, relocation, and swapping of territories, and it is something that cannot be avoided." Was that view expressed by Mr. Srdic? By this time, mid-February, was that a widespread view among deputies in the Serb assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that this will be misunderstood. The previous participant in the discussion said that the Krajina, the Krajina option, the Krajina that was autonomous, should be a state, and Mr. Srdic is saying or rather he is opposing that, and he says, "Our decision reached by plebiscite is different." Although he didn't say this, but creating states within Bosnia-Herzegovina would lead to relocation and so on and so forth. If you remember once we read something to that effect here when Mr. Karadzic said something like that and he's against that option. He thinks that what Mr. Sidjak said was better. So the meaning of what Mr. Srdic said was to oppose this discussion that we are now supposed to create some kind of princely states. Rather, Bosnia should be transformed into three national, constituent units. If you saw this up here, perhaps it is hard to understand, this other one talks about Sarajevo, and he says, Mr. Sidjak, that he is particularly against having its seat in Sarajevo. All of these phrases are just inserted, so they have a different interpretation when I read it, I who understand the language, than when this is interpreted or translated. The point of what he was saying was not to create states within Bosnia-Herzegovina because that would lead to relocations and so on and so forth. You can analyse everything here and you will see that that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient point for Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, may I hand to Mr. Krajisnik through the usual channels -- it's the 7th session, transcript of the 7th session of the Serb Assembly, 15th February 2002, and keeping my fingers crossed, Your Honour, it's P65, binder 8, tab 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you go, please, Mr. Krajisnik, to page 15?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've numbered that in the margin one, and you as the president chairing this session, you introduced the session, and you're there and we see this throughout this meeting at this point you're you the meeting are discussing the draft constitution for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the draft in -- Professor Milanovic is talking and he says, do you see, third paragraph of what he's saying, with respect to Article 3, and the definition of the Bosnia-Herzegovina territory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page in English would be, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's 15, Your Honour. I'm sorry, Your Honour, did I not say that? I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He says with respect to Article 3 and the definition of the BH territory, "let me tell you what I have proposed at the meetings of our constitutional commission, of which I am a member." "Mr. Krajisnik, we had difficulty finding that draft that was before the meeting. What we do have is the constitution as adopted."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's P64 A, tab 551, binder 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, that shows, and perhaps you could say if it's your recollection, that was the provision under discussion, a very simple form of Article 3, just stating the republic is a part of the federal state of Yugoslavia. Do you recall that was -- that was the very short, simple statement in Article 3 as adopted, but Article 2 of the constitution, as it was adopted, and we are jumping ahead here, said the territory of the republic consists of Serb autonomous regions, municipalities and other Serb ethnic entities, including the regions in which genocide was committed against the Serb people in the Second World War. We've come across that wording before, broadly in that form, but do you recall that that was what was adopted as the definition of the territory of the republic in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to both your questions is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go to -- you can go straight on to page 23. And the speaker is Mr. Zekic, Mr. Goran Zekic. I put the note number 2 in the margin. He says, "I have skipped a reference to the territory of the republic. This Article 3 has been outlined so that it leaves open the possibility for most Serbian territories and areas to become parts of Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina but this is a realistic version of a peaceful resolution to the situation. Perhaps we should still include a reference to a historical standard, a reference to territories that belonged to us once historically. In case of conflict, for instance, the constitution would provide for the possibility that the territories which used to be ours but were lost not only as a result of genocide but because of migrations, too, but which are necessary. For instance, this stretch along the Drina, to connect Romanija with Serbia and others, we must take them and make a breakthrough, we should not deprive ourselves in advance of this possibility or giving up claiming such standards in case of a different outcome in this situation." So, Mr. Krajisnik, it appears, but say immediately if this is wrong, beyond the definition which incorporates the regions in which genocide was committed against the Serb people in the second world war, Mr. Zekic is suggesting something in addition to that by reference to historic territories which had been lost; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were various proposals. One of them was the one you just mentioned. Historically, some areas were populated by one ethnic community, then by another, then there were migrations. So it was not very clear but he probably meant Srebrenica and the Drina valley where he comes from. That's probably the reason why he spoke as he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But his view was not accepted, and not therefore adopted in the constitution, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was not included because there were reasons. We wanted to stretch our hand, to reach out to the other side once again, wanting this constitution to be the constitution of all the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although the decision on referendum had already been taken. The constitution was only proclaimed on the 22nd of March 1992. As for the draft, I have that copy with me. I can give it to you if you're interested, although I don't think that's necessary. I have one copy of the draft as it was in the first version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you're saying you actually have the draft with you here today, well, yes, as a matter of fact, I would be interested, with the Trial Chamber's permission.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not here. I have it in my room at the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Stewart, if you're interested that you'll still be interested tomorrow if Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I will remain interested tomorrow, Your Honour, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could bring it, Mr. Krajisnik, that would be highly appreciated by Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we go on, then, to -- it's page 26 in the Serbian. It's top of page 27 in the English. It's margin number 4, and it's Mr. Milojevic speaking with regards to Article 3. Mr. Krajisnik, I think we are going to find that Article 3 gets renumbered as Article 2 in the constitution as it emerges, when you bring the draft tomorrow. You're nodding but we are going to find that that there was a renumbering, I think. But with regards to Article 3, "this morning I looked up the borders on the map. Please let us give this Article serious examination once more. I am not sure that I could mark borders on the map on the basis of the present Article 3. We should first consider the concept of Serbian ethnic areas." Mr. Krajisnik, on the basis of an article number 2 or 3, that talked about regions in which genocide was committed against the Serb people in the Second World War, would you have been confidently able to mark definite borders of the territory of the Serb republic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the map as to where the genocide was committed is included in the documentation of the OTP. It is documented. One of the maps is attached. It wasn't the point here, nor was I able to draw the borders then. The point was that this was being discussed during the talks with Mr. Cutileiro, and you have pressure for Krajina to be formed, and there were also actions aimed at stopping a process that we were reluctant to support, the breaking up of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we were proceeding in gradual steps as long as it was possible to find a solution through talks with Mr. Cutileiro. So this was a time when the talks were already far advanced and it was already known what the criteria were, et cetera. That's why people were talking about ethnic areas and other entities. So this was a time when the talks on Bosnia and Herzegovina were already under way under the aegis of the European Community talks on Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The position is this, Mr. Krajisnik, that the adoption of -- and it was adopted, the adoption of a constitution containing a definition of the territory of the Serb republic was done in circumstances where there was at least considerable room for doubt as to where exactly one would draw the boundaries of that territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right. It's a different matter that each of those who contributed to the discussion saw that map differently but it was impossible to discuss borders without an agreement between the three sides. That was always a requirement. You couldn't simply say "these are our territories," and that's it. It was impossible, at least from the view point of the Serbian side. That was our official position, which is different, of course, from the position of certain individuals. Everybody by the way wanted their village to be in the Serbian part of the territory. That's why this was worded in such a general way, to make it amenable to stretching because it was a matter for negotiation. It was not only up to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go about -- it's about a dozen lines down in the English, I hope it won't be too different in the Serbian, but there is a reference to 51 per cent, should be a figure, and a sentence that begins, "We should say that we shall grant the right of absolute ethnic majority." Do you see that sentence? There is a reference to the phrase, 'absolute ethnic majority.' Then this follows that. Do you have that point, Mr. Krajisnik? It's only about a dozen lines after where the number 4 has been marked in the margin.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's page 27 in Serbian, where you see 31 per cent and 51 per cent on the same page, if that's the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A few lines above that, then, it says, "We shall say that we shall grant the right of absolute ethnic majority to others just as we claim the absolute ethnic majority right for ourselves as the criterion for the determination of the sovereignty of a people. I think that this may be the sole criterion because only where it makes an absolute ethnic majority can a people be considered a sovereign people or make sovereign decisions without asking the others. I think that only through the inclusion of this (I am just bringing this forth for discussion because I think it is very important), the inclusion of the absolute ethnic majority criterion as the criterion of delineation, the physical delineation between us and them, we should accept one thing. We cannot transform our 31 per cent of the people into 51 per cent (interjections from the Benches). They will be a minority among us just as in some areas, we will be a minority among them." Interjections on the benches? Did that signify some degree of dissent or opposition to what Mr. Milojevic was saying there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember this correctly, they were opposed to this reference of 31 per cent because the opinion prevailed that a large number of Serbs had declared themselves as Yugoslavs in the census, 31.5 per cent were nominally Serbs, 43 per cent of Muslims, and 17.5 per cent of Croats. But there was a large number of Yugoslavs, and the ace of Mr. Milojevic was that we couldn't rely on 31.5 per cent as being the true number of Serbs. He was saying, we have 51 actually, because we had most of the land, 64 per cent. So he was opposed to the 31 per cent as being taken as the figure. The Serbs were the most numerous people in Yugoslavia so many of them declared themselves as Yugoslavs. Some Croats did as well but it is true that it was mostly Serbs who put themselves into the category of Yugoslavs and other people after those present did not approve his argument. They didn't approve even what he said earlier about the absolute majority. The relative majority was supposed to be the criterion whereas somebody would have 40 per cent, 30 per cent; 43 per cent should have been the decisive figure. Even what he said about, you know, they were going to be a minority in our area and we were going to be a minority in their area, it's certainly not right that we should make decisions without asking the others. I think he went too far. He is a nice man, a Professor, but I think he went too far in his philosophising, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to seek clarification, Mr. Krajisnik, of something you said. It's at line 19 of the transcript. You said he, that's Mr. Milojevic was saying we have 51 per cent actually because we had most of the land of the just looking at the text here, he says, "we should accept one thing, we cannot transform our 31 per cent of the people into 51 per cent, they will be a minority among us, just as in some areas we will be a minority among them." Mr. Krajisnik, it's not perhaps a hundred per cent clear. When you say that Mr. Milojevic was saying we have 51 actually, and he was opposed to 31 per cent being taken as the figure, the English reading tends to suggest the opposite. That's why I'm -- unless you're going to explain a misunderstanding there, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I just heard this interpreted to me, it's exactly the opposite. The figure, 31 per cent, or 31.5, never mind, that's the percentage according to the 1991 census, the percentage of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And now when I was talking about 31 and why that caused a reaction, I explained that it was because of Yugoslavs. Let me not repeat myself. But here, Mr. Milojevic says speaking of the territories that probably the preceding speakers discussed, said, "We cannot transform our 31 per cent and present it as if we made up 51 per cent." That's the point he was making. And it's only later the territories are discussed because we were not dividing population. What I mean to say is that we were not talking about separating the population but about delineating between territories and that's the difference between those maps, if you remember, that I mentioned. So your observation is completely correct. It was a misunderstanding. He was saying we cannot say 51 per cent of the population and we want more territory than we have. That's what caused a reaction from outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One additional clarification, when you mentioned the 64 per cent, that was your own observation in this respect? Is that your comment to it? Because I do not see anyone speaking about 64 per cent. So I understand that that was your own observation in relation to this matter discussed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's -- that was my comment indeed. I don't know whether it features in his contribution but we bandied about that figure quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He then says, "This is a reality of life. We shall regulate our interactions at the level of the republic on the basis of reciprocity and we shall claim reciprocal rights. We must accept that there will be areas where Serbs will be a minority. But Croats or Muslims will be a minority in other areas. Excuse me, but in some of the purest Serbian areas, we have only 60 per cent Serbs. Others make the remaining 40 per cent. This is life, and this is the reality of life that we are witness to and must have it reflected in the constitution, that we will be both a minority and a majority, that they will also be both a minority and a majority, and that on the basis of a physical demarcation of our separate sovereignties and on the basis of reciprocal rights we will be able to arrange some kind of interaction right from the beginning." Mr. Krajisnik, that passage that I've just read, did that match the intentions and approach of the negotiating team that were about to resume talking to Mr. Cutileiro and others?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the official policy and the subject of our discussions with Mr. Cutileiro, namely that certain ethnic communities will be in the minority in some areas but that there should be reciprocity and so on and so forth. So what Mr. Milojevic said stands, and he advocated it. Plus we advanced that as a necessary condition in our talks with Mr. Cutileiro. We knew that Serbs would be a minority in some Muslim areas, for instance, and we had nothing against that as long as their ethnic rights were protected as well as their human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, he continues, and it's at the very foot of page 27 of the English, slightly different page in the Serbian but it's immediately following that passage. "We cannot know what is coming 50 years from now." Do you see that reference, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "We can cannot know what is copping 50 years from now. Let us leave that to the process of time. We do not know whether there will be resettlements or cleansing of ethnic territory or if we are to reach such a stage of civilisation where it is irrelevant whether we are in a minority or a majority, but at this stage, we should opt for the criterion of ethnic majority and an acceptance of the ethnic minority." What did you understand Mr. Milojevic to be talking about when he used the phrase there, "Cleansing of ethnic territory"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly what kind of debate was going on then. Deputies from the Bosnian Krajina, that means Krajina in Bosnia, were saying that there were whole areas that were predominantly Serb. They mentioned Cazin, Bihac, Prijedor, and so on, and they were saying that that people was ethnically cleansed, meaning killed, in the Second World War. And after the war, there were migrations also to Vojvodina and to Slavonia. There were some immoderate qualifications uttered there. And Mr. Milojevic made his point in the first sentence. "Let us -- wait and see what happens in 50 years. Time will show. What we should deal now is our current problem, the one that's on the table now. And we should concentrate on the transformation of Bosnia and Herzegovina." It's not as if he was advocating ethnic cleansing. He was invoking the genocide that took place in World War II in his reply to deputies from Bosnian Krajina. I'm just trying to explain what kind of a debate it was, because they were saying that it was many years before the first soldier from that area that was cleansed in World War II went to join the army. That's the extent to which the men had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then at page 30, and it's apparently 30 of both the English and the version in your language, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic speaks. There should be a number 6 in the margin against where he begins. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the third paragraph of Dr. Karadzic's distribution there, he says, "With regard to majorities, many areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina would remain undefined in this respect because no group can claim absolute majority in them. I think that where we have a majority we should not be mentioning whether we have an absolute or relative majority but only refer to areas where Serbs constitute a majority. There are areas and we arranged with one of our partners that in the area where they represent a relative majority we will vote so that the area is defined as theirs and that they will do the same with their vote in those areas where we constitute a relative majority. After all, the maps are surely going to be the subject of negotiation and of some dispute. It would be so much better if these are political rather than of some other kind, and I do think that it is entirely possible." Mr. Krajisnik, he says there, Dr. Karadzic, we arranged with one of our partners that in the area where they represent a relative majority we will vote so that the area is defined as theirs.
