He's talking there, is he, about -- well, either Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say yes, perhaps, although I believe that Mr. Karadzic was a bit closer to Croats there. There were more talks with the Croat side than with the Muslim side. As for what Mr. Karadzic was saying, that was the version before, not the final version. If there are 33 per cent Serbs, 33 per cent Croats, and 33 per cent Muslims, where nobody has either a relative or an absolute majority. So the three ethnic communities should agree to which area one place belongs. For instance, Muslims and Croats say, Together we form 66 per cent; this place should go into this territorial unit. So Karadzic was referring to one of the other two sides here and we were saying that some areas -- they were saying that some areas should go to the Croat side and some areas to our side, in order to round off the territories. That was the territorial principle advocated in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go on to page 37 in the English. It's page 38 in your version, Mr. Krajisnik, you should find the number 8 in the margin.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is Professor Kosutic talking. I don't think we have come across him before. Who was he, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a professor of the University of Belgrade, a professor of law. I mean, he's a trained lawyer. He was invited to help our lawyers, and he attended this session and he gave a contribution with regard to the constitution. Actually, he was asked to come in through private channels, if I can put it that way. He was pretty close to Mr. Karadzic so he invited him to come to be a sort of adviser to us so that we avoid mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if we go against the margin number 8, where he is speaking at the page 37, English, page 38, in your version, Mr. Krajisnik, he says the first matter relates to the referendum question. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "The people has decided in favour of living in a common state with those people who wish the same. This must be stated. The country referred to is called Yugoslavia. Naturally, it is possible that the name will change later, if the proper authorities so wish, but that is irrelevant. In this moment, the country is Yugoslavia and that is the name it was referred to as in the referendum question. Similarly you are keeping to your own words that you are absolutely not against living in a common Bosnia and Herzegovina under the provision that it be a state of three equal peoples." And Mr. Krajisnik, the constitution, as it was adopted at that meeting, stated baldly in article 3, the republic is a part of the federal state of Yugoslavia. Had you got an indication from Belgrade -- and I don't mean with respect to the academics in Belgrade, such as this Professor, but from the political leaders in Belgrade, of their attitude towards that provision being included in your Bosnian Serb constitution?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision was a definite one, as I've already said. I said that a few days ago. To establish a new Yugoslavia and that we could not be in it because of the position taken by the conference on Yugoslavia. That Yugoslavia had not been established yet. I think it was only in April. I can't remember exactly when it was promulgated. I remember this very well. In the draft, this was yet another argument in our talks with the other sides, although we were quite aware of the fact that we could not be in Yugoslavia because quite simply Yugoslavia would be established along different lines. Mr. Kosutic probably mentioned that in his talks with Mr. Karadzic. I don't think that it wasn't that he wasn't informed by him. He was saying, well, you stay in Bosnia, then he explained that model, but they didn't want to discourage people who kept saying, well, we had a plebiscite. Why are you now in the constitution throwing us out of Yugoslavia? It's not a problem. We can promulgate the constitution later. Let's find a solution for Bosnia and Herzegovina. It's going to be easy for us to turn this constitution of ours into something that would be incorporated into the documents of the internationally recognised state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think I can remember all of this pretty well. Maybe I can make a mistake but I know what our wish was, to have these negotiations and to have a solution. And indeed, what followed later were some steps forward in that regard. Positive steps forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then there is a contribution from Dr. Kalinic, and this is probably -- probably begins at page 57 or just possibly 56 in your version, Mr. Krajisnik, but in the English it's at the top of page 54. Dr. Kalinic begins to speak. Do you find where he starts, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it. And I see the number 9 after that, where Mr. Kalinic begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. You do see the number 9. I'm actually going to start earlier, though, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm going to start near the beginning of Dr. Kalinic's contribution. But summarising, he says, Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, I will give a few proposals. Then the essence of the first long paragraph is got from somewhere in the middle where he says, "I strongly believe we should really hurry up the work on the constitution, aware that this constitution is not the first or the last one," but I'm not going to dwell on that paragraph. The next paragraph he says, "The other thing I wanted to suggest seems much more important. We shall have a constitution but it remains questionable whether our state will begin to function. Earlier today, in a smaller group, I suggested a medical procedure. You know that our ministers, our council of ministers, with Mr. Cizmovic and Mr. Simovic, are to tour all our municipalities and establish the true situation during the next seven days, which would help us determine whether we have an infrastructure which may become operational once we proclaim our Serbian Republic or not. We cannot be sovereign if we are not able to exercise power over the territory that is ours." First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, can you say in his reference to a smaller group, was Dr. Kalinic referring to a group of which -- in which you had been a participant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know who it was he was talking to. He could have talked to his MPs from the reformist forces or somebody else. I mean, I don't remember any such idea being voiced at any meeting that I attended. And I believe that he talked to somebody else, some circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did you, at this point, before Dr. Kalinic spoke at this assembly meeting, did you know of this plan or proposal for Mr. Cizmovic, Mr. Simovic, and maybe others, to tour all our municipalities and establish the true situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm convinced that I did not know about anything like that. I know that they didn't go and visit later so it was just a proposal of his. I believe this was just a contribution to the discussion, some proposal of his by way of a contribution to this strengthening but that was not adopted and it was not carried through, and I do not remember Mr. Cizmovic and Mr. Simovic visiting those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then I'll go to the next paragraph. He begins, "The third thing that I'm really uneasy about." Do you find that, Mr. Krajisnik, that will be at page 58?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 55 in the English. "The third thing that I'm really uneasy about has bothered me since the last time and I can see that no progress has been made, but perhaps the gentlemen from the inner circles of leaders of the Serbian party may have more to say about it. I can see that the constitution provides for the JNA to take on the defence. I wish to God it was this simple or easy to achieve. I think that the next seven days should be used for something else, something we said in our previous conclusion, that our relationship with the Yugoslav People's Army should be redefined in terms of determining the common ground in our political and essential interests and that we have urgent talks with General Staff and ask them whether the Yugoslav People's Army will be ready on the 23rd or worse yet on the 29th or the 30th when Bosnia and Herzegovina will be declared an independent country, something I have no doubt will happen because all that has been arranged and stored in computers. We should ask them whether they would defend the territories of the Serbian people, that is the territories that belong to the common state of Yugoslavia." So first of all, Mr. -- Dr. Kalinic is -- he's offering what from the Bosnian Serb point of view is a relatively gloomy prediction, isn't he, that independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina may well be declared later that same month?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kalinic is panic-mongering here and unfortunately that actually happened. He was speaking in a panic-stricken way, that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be recognised, that there would be a war. It was the 30th, I think, probably. It's February. So it couldn't have been the 30th of February. It had to be the 30th of March. So we had to see whether the Yugoslav People's Army, whether they would protect us, as we had planned, as our position was, and whether they will not do that. All of this is panic-stricken thinking, and unfortunately in part he proved to be right ultimately because we really did not believe that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be recognised before the transformation is adopted, just as Mr. Cutileiro told us exactly. We would carry out this transformation, we would go for a referendum, after this transformation, and then that would be the end. I have an article from that period of time. He said first the referendum and then the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina but a referendum about this joint proposal of all three sides. So what he proposed that we should establish some new variant, that is to say some Territorial Defence or something like that. All of that is confusing and a product of his concern, which regrettably was rather well founded too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, as a matter of fact I hadn't overlooked the technicality that February, as usual, didn't have a 30th, though it did have a 29th that year, by the way. But whether he was thinking of a particular month, he was -- is correct, is he, that you -- it's correct, is it, you understood that Dr. Kalinic was saying it's going to happen very soon, independence being declared?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There were some intimations, if I can put it that way, some tangible and realistic ones, that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be recognised. Mr. Kalinic is right on that, so this additional warning addressed to the international community and making people aware of our constitution was aimed at that. Let us agree on this transformation first so that we would resolve the problem by peaceful means. We don't need the situation to deteriorate any further. So you're right, yes, there were quite a few indications that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be proclaimed an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, so far as you knew at the time of this assembly session, had anybody among the Bosnian Serb leadership already had any discussions with the General Staff of the JNA about what would happen or would be done if and when Bosnia and Herzegovina was declared an independent country?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not talk about that variant, but the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I don't know exactly in which period of time, talked about this in Sarajevo and in Skopje about this, with the General Staff, that is to say about the fate of the Yugoslav People's Army in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for us, the Serb side, whether we talked to the JNA and to the General Staff, about this variant, what would happen if Bosnia-Herzegovina were to be recognised, are you going to defend us? I know, or rather I don't know about that kind of variant. And I'm sure that nobody talked about this because this went without saying. They would carry out their constitutional role. That's what we wanted. That's the way we wanted to. There should be no war and that there should be a transformation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and up to that moment the JNA should safeguard the peace and if there are attacks then they should defend themselves. If you remember, at one point Karadzic says we don't need an army, we have the Yugoslav People's Army, that promised to defend those who are attacked, and since we are not going to attack anyone, then they are going to defend the Serb people. It's in a statement that he made. I think that it was presented here too. So it should carry out its constitutional function. The Yugoslav People's Army should carry out its constitutional function.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we appreciate you're not a lawyer, but your answer said they would carry out their constitutional role. From your point of view, as a politician and economist, not a lawyer, in those circumstances, where Bosnia and Herzegovina declared itself independent and let us hypothesise was recognised as independent by -- sufficient of the international community, what did you perceive to be the constitutional role of the JNA from that moment?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, our understanding was that we did not accept that recognition. For us it was unlawful recognition because it was done in an unlawful way. It is well known the constitution says what the role of the JNA is. Now, what were we thinking? We wanted part of that authority that had to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina, should -- would mean that the JNA would be there as the only remaining armed force, that they should protect those who are protected, to preserve the peace. That is what we had in mind. It is not for me to say. And it was not for anyone of us to say that Yugoslavia should be protected and many others but as far as Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, we expected them to protect the peace and if anyone were to be attacked, to protect them, that they should be there sort of as a buffer. That is the point of what I'm saying, that this is constitutional subject matter, but certainly this does not exhaust it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It should read those who are attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, from your standpoint, and you made this very clear, Mr. Krajisnik, a declaration of independence, recognised albeit by the international community, from your standpoint was unlawful. I'm simply noting what you have clearly said in that vein. Was -- well, I haven't asked a question yet, Mr. Krajisnik. That's -- have I misrepresented your position, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You presented my position quite rightly, although perhaps some additions would be needed. Even today I think that Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised in an unconstitutional manner. It should have been done in the assembly and then the constitution changed. Mr. Filipovic wrote a book. I can slow it to you. I can show you what his comments are in terms of how all of that was done then. It was not constitutional. Well, but that's the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm certainly not trying to conduct a legal seminar here so my questions are directed towards -- well, your position as a politician. Perhaps make that clear. Did you -- did you seek advice from lawyers at this point, this assembly session, 15th of February, had you sought advice from lawyers as to what the constitutional position of the JNA would be in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we did not discuss the JNA at any length because it was there. There was a provision in our talks with Mr. Cutileiro that as for the question of defence we would regulate it separately. Let me just add something to what I've already said. When I said a few moments ago that we did not recognise that way of recognising Bosnia-Herzegovina, at that moment we said, "Let Bosnia be recognised but we want it to be transformed now because that was promised to us. We want that process to be carried through, internationally recognised, to complete the Cutileiro plan." So after all, the UN recognised the country but we asked for it to be transformed and to finally bring this process and this crisis to an end. We were against a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, the kind that was recognised, but we were not against a Bosnia-Herzegovina that would have been transformed as had been proposed by the European Community. So that was the meaning involved. As for seeking advice from lawyers, since this is a question of the constitution, eminent lawyers took part in the debate on the constitution itself. As for the JNA, it went without saying that it would remain there during some transition period so we did not debate that. I don't even know whether we asked them but I don't think so. It wasn't necessary in our view.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps to avoid any possibility of cross-purposes, when you talk about the constitutional role of the JNA, you say it was well known the constitution says what the role of the JNA is. Were you referring to the newly adopted constitution of the Serb republic or the constitution of federal Yugoslavia, as it had already been existing?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, that former Yugoslavia still existed, not the newly established one. So according to that constitution, the Yugoslav People's Army had its constitutional role. That's what I meant. Because we were not authorised to envisage the role of the Yugoslav People's Army. It was not under our command and we didn't have the right to do that. We are taking the facts as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So is it the position that you were relying upon also in the sense of leaving it to the JNA to implement or carry out their constitutional role, without guidance, direction, request, from you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we did not have the ability to influence them. Perhaps there were some individuals who thought that they were the best military leaders possible, but our position was that we seek information as to how the Yugoslav People's Army would behave but we could not make any suggestions and we could not order them, and that indeed was not done. We became its natural ally because the other two sides turned against the Yugoslav People's Army, sealed off their barracks, waged war on them and so on. So we were closing to the Yugoslav People's Army then and we could have some information. As for guidelines regarding its moves, its action, we didn't do that and we couldn't have done any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, is this correct, Mr. Krajisnik, that at this time, and I'm still talking about 15th February, when you were holding this assembly session, you were as we know about to have further meeting and talks with Mr. Cutileiro and others, your evidence to the Trial Chamber has been that you wished and in your case at least, Mr. Krajisnik, you told the Trial Chamber you were really rather hopeful that some positive, peaceful solution would emerge from that, that that's right so far, isn't it, as a summary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely right, and there was a solution. In March a solution had been found. If you remember the first version of the Lisbon agreement and then the Sarajevo agreement. So that indeed followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll come to those, Mr. Krajisnik. But at this point in time, in February, with that being summarised as your position, there nevertheless was, wasn't there, lurking there the distinct possibility that before that process could come to a successful conclusion, it would be pre-empted by a declaration of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina recognised by the international community? That -- Dr. Kalinic may have had that fear more strongly than others but it was a distinct possibility lurking there in your minds, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. I've been saying Mr. Stewart is right so often that I'm afraid I'll be hard put to say differently in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm reeling from the shock, Mr. Krajisnik, but I'll recover. Mr. Krajisnik, if that did happen, what, in your mind, at that time, in February, would be the need or the trigger for any action by any military forces?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what happened. I'm not going to say now what happened in the beginning of April -- sorry, yeah, beginning of April, although you will probably ask me, but if the proclamation of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina happened without the realisation of the European promise that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be first transformed into three entities, that would have meant that somebody else's solution was imposed on us, and it was unpredictable what could happen. I don't think that anybody on our side would have made any moves towards war, but just as war began in April, in a spontaneous, or shall I say uncontrolled way, we were afraid of exactly the same thing when we were at that assembly session. There was a lot of armed people, there were armed forces, and weapons are never silent. The JNA later withdrew, paramilitary units appeared. It doesn't take much for the entire Bosnia to be set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what -- Mr. Krajisnik, I appreciate in the light of the fact that all sorts of things did happen and sometimes it's not absolutely straightforward to turn your mind back to the middle of February before they happened, but as best you can do, I'm asking you at this time in the middle of February, for the senior figures among the Bosnian Serbs, what was your real fear as to what would happen if this declaration and recognition of independence did pre-empt the peace discussions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Publicly, when we debated, everybody was saying that that could never happen, and even if it did we wouldn't recognise it. People did not admit to fear easily. I'll tell you what I felt and what I thought, I personally. As I said before, I thought we were going to find a solution, and I was afraid of war. When I say I was afraid of war, I mean I was afraid of the stories I'd been hearing about what war brings with it, and I saw that everybody on the Serb leadership was concerned that such a unilateral move could lead to uncontrolled moves that would be made by people on the local level about which you cannot do anything. So you conduct a two-pronged policy. You keep telling your collocutors that something will be done, there will be no war, and then when something happens, you have to hear them tell you, yesterday you were telling me one thing, today you're telling me quite another, see what happened, et cetera. All sorts of information was flowing in. So we were making this move geared solely at negotiations. We were saying that we had drafted this constitution but we will proclaim it only at a later stage, wanting to find a solution in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did -- was Dr. Kalinic's request or suggestion that there should be urgent talks with the General Staff adopted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was adopted or not. I attended another meeting when the leadership or rather the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina talked to representatives of the General Staff in Sarajevo. I attended that one but not any other. Even if something like that had been adopted, it wasn't carried out. I'm sure it wasn't carried out anywhere outside Sarajevo, outside this meeting. There were contacts with Mr. Kukanjac, who was there in Sarajevo. All the sides had contacts with him but he is not the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Without my proposing to explore it immediately, Mr. Krajisnik, but just so we can be clear, when you referred a moment ago to a meeting that you did attend with representatives of the General Staff in Sarajevo, when was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the date but I know it was around that time. There was Mr. Brovet, Mr. Adzic, and Mr. Kadijevic. I think that was the composition of the delegation of the General Staff, and on the other side, there were representatives of BH, the president of the assembly, the Prime Minister, the president of the Presidency. I cannot name any others, I'm afraid. I could make a mistake. But it's documented somewhere and the media wrote about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Before or after this assembly session? Are you able to say that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have to be honest. Logically, it should have been after, but I can't remember when it was held. Plus, this meeting did not discuss the topic raised by Mr. Kalinic. It was not about are you going to defend the Serb people? It was just a meeting with representatives of the General Staff. I don't remember that we ever talked with the General Staff about this proposal put forward by Mr. Kalinic. I don't remember that we ever asked them, can you protect us? Will you defend us? If not, we are going to establish our own army. I am certain I would have remembered if the Serbian side had discussed it with the General Staff, ever. It went without saying, as I already said, that they would defend whatever party is attacked, and in the meantime, we were looking for a political solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At this time, in -- right in the middle of February 1992, did Mr. Ratko Mladic have an active role in the politics of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't think so. At least not until the establishment of the army of Republika Srpska. But before he became commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, he did replace General Kukanjac as commander of the 2nd military district and before that he was co-commander in Knin which covered a larger area, including a bit into Bosnia and Herzegovina. I met him for the first time at the discussions concerning the Vance-Owen plan and after that I didn't see him again for a long time but politically speaking, I had never heard that name. I didn't know him. I wasn't aware of him, although I'd heard about him, but he didn't play any role.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So let's be clear. You had mentioned specifically earlier this morning that he'd been in Belgrade for that meeting or those meetings involving Mr. Babic. You said that, Mr. Krajisnik. I've just said a moment ago that was the first time you met him. So you had not seen or met him at all in the couple of weeks since the Belgrade meeting when we get to this assembly on the 15th of February; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't meet with him before. I met him only then. He occupied some sort of position in Knin. I didn't talk to him. I didn't know him, until he replaced Kukanjac. I don't know when that was exactly, but after that I saw him twice, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is -- was the next time that you ever saw Mr. Mladic after you went -- moved to Pale in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's that period, yes. I think after he replaced Mr. Kukanjac, after that incident happened in Sarajevo when the command was being withdrawn, he came to replace Kukanjac and he was probably working on the withdrawal of other barracks, and I must have seen him then. You're right. That's that time. I hadn't seen him before that, because I know that he had met with Mr. Kukanjac before. He led me through the barricades to my home in Zabrdje, so until the war began, I didn't see Mr. Mladic. It's all coming back to me, especially some events.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the time of this assembly session on the 15th of February 1992, had you personally, Mr. Krajisnik, been involved in any war planning for the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I'm convinced that none of the Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina worked on any plan. There was absolutely no military plan except for the JNA. I can say that with 100 per cent certainty, because I should have known if anybody had planned anything militarily. I'm talking about the civilian side. The Yugoslav People's Army is something different and we didn't have anything official to do with them. There was some SDS support to the army in their move for mobilisation but we did not plan anything with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let me clarify by broadening the question a bit, Mr. Krajisnik. When I ask whether you had been involved in any war planning, I'm extending the question to include any form of civil defence planning or war preparations as well as purely armed forces planning. Do you -- is the question clear to you, extended in that way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just ask whether I understand the question? Are you referring -- perhaps among other matters -- to distribution of arms among Serbians? Would you like to include such an event, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sure I would include that, Your Honour, in that question, yes. I was trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, many words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Express it as neutrally as I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, but that's the core of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least it's an important part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One of the matters, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when you said that you should have known if anybody had planned anything militarily, would you include, and where you said I'm convinced that none of the Serbs from Bosnia and Herzegovina worked on any plan, would that include any form of distribution of arms among civilians or at least outside the JNA or the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am -- I've been on guard all the time, fearing any kind of imprecision, but I did allow an imprecision. What I meant to say is that it would have been logical for me to have been informed, but as to whether arms were distributed or not, I know how people received arms. Krsman mentioned it. I'm talking about something that was official, and when we talked, maybe in the council, at the club, in assembly sessions, I never attended a meeting that would have discussed military organising. Two things did happen at the session of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. An issue was raised concerning an incident on two occasions two trucks or rather several times trucks carrying weapons were intercepted. Once the Serb side was blamed in Herzegovina and in Sarajevo. I simply didn't get involved in that. That was up to the MUP and the Prosecutor's office and others. I'm speaking from me personally. We had a plan in Bosnia-Herzegovina, a contingency plan, in case the war broke out. I had that plan, as the speaker of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was in my drawer. That's something that existed for Bosnia-Herzegovina. As to whether the Serb side militarily organised something, made any plans, I completely ignored all about it at that time. Maybe somebody else was planning something at the time. I am receiving all sorts of information now but I did not know anything about it then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask when you said I received all sorts of information but you did not know anything about it, then are you referring to later moments that you received all sorts of information or were you talking about what happened at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I observe, Your Honour in my transcript it does very specifically say "now."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the transcript he said, "I'm receiving all sorts of information now but I did not know anything about it then," which seems clearly to deal with the point Your Honour just raised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I've overlooked that, then -- let me just check. Yes. I see that. My question was superfluous. I should not have put it to you because you have been clear enough, Mr. Krajisnik. I apologise. Please proceed Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart is right again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I worry about that, Your Honour. On that note, Your Honour, I see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn. We'll resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, there was one matter of clarification that I'd like to ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this morning you spent some time on explaining to us that you would have an absolute majority situation or a relative majority situation where one of the ethnic groups would be the largest one but less than 50 per cent. Now, yesterday you explained to us in relation to the document, the variations A and B document, that there would be no need at all to take certain measures in Variant A majority Serb municipalities because it was more or less the existing situation that they had a majority so therefore they could exercise all these powers or authority on the basis of the existing situation. May I take it from that explanation that you interpreted the Variant A and B document where it speaks about majority Serb, that that would be an absolute majority Serb situation? Is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You are quite right. Variant B was for municipalities where Serbs had 51 per cent of deputies in the municipal assembly. 51 per cent or more. That's about Variant A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. A, not B, yes. So majority municipality would mean absolute majority. Okay. Thank you very much for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there was talk about the municipal assembly here, where you have 51 per cent of the power, meaning deputies. That's where you have proportionate power. But the consequence was what you just said, that Serbs voted for Serbs, Muslims for Muslims, Croats for Croats. So the municipality where we had power was where we had 51 per cent of the deputies, therefore majority power. There was no talk about ethnic composition but the two were linked. They coincided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear to me. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can we move on to the next point in this same document, which is at page 61 of your version and it's at page 58 of the English. I've marked it as point 10.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's Dr. Karadzic speaking, and he says, "Something tells me that Mr. Krajisnik is going to conclude the proceedings soon. So I would make two requests." Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "The first request is addressed to Krajina deputies. I am asking them to work a lot with our people there, with party membership, to explain our strategic goals and to explain our tactics on a daily basis. Even if we have not changed our tactics that much, we went straight through the mountain so that our people can clearly see what we are about." Were there at that time, Mr. Krajisnik, identifiable, formulated strategic goals of the Bosnian Serb leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is evident here that Mr. Karadzic is asking nicely the deputies from Krajina, meaning Banja Luka Krajina, which was, as I said before, the Bosnian part of Krajina, to explain what we had been talking about that day, that we want a unified republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that the version of Krajina that they often wanted to put forward as their own version was not our strategic goal. When he talks about strategic goals, he means that tactically speaking, we should be saying something to be interpreted by something else, whereas we were talking straightforwardly. We want Yugoslavia, we want a constituent unit in Bosnia. So that was our strategic goal, to have one single unified constituent unit within Bosnia-Herzegovina. At this moment, it was proclaimed in the Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So Mr. Karadzic asked the deputies to explain our goal, our current goal, to the Serbian people in Krajina. You remember the conclusions of the Autonomous Region of Krajina within Yugoslavia. So this was an attempt to explain what happened at this session. It's almost identical to what was adopted on the 12th of May but we'll deal with that later. So our goal was to explain to the people on the ground everything that was discussed at that session that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, we will certainly come to it in the course of your evidence. It's not my intention to go two or three months on and launch into an exploration of those 12th of May goals now but where you say in that answer, "It's almost identical to what was adopted on the 12th of May," what specifically at this point is almost identical to what was adopted on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we follow the sequence of events, we have a constitution here which, for political reasons, refers to Yugoslavia, but what was discussed was the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was in the Cutileiro plan something that was supposed to be called the Serbian constituent unit in Bosnia and Herzegovina on a par with the Muslim and Croat constituent units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So Mr. Karadzic is saying, "Please explain that all of us Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina will have one constituent unit. It will not be your region that will form the constituent unit." Of course, that needed explaining because people had already gotten used to their identity as a region. And that was closely linked with our talks, negotiations with Mr. Cutileiro. But politically speaking we were preparing the ground rather than saying to the people abruptly, "We cannot be part of that Yugoslavia that hasn't even been formed by that time." That's what I think is rather similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm leaving this document now, Mr. Krajisnik, and Your Honours, so you can put that on one side, the assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Stewart, I had great difficulties in following your numbering in the B/C/S version, never any of the pages you mentioned I found. There seems to be perhaps a problem in the original as well, as far as paging is concern. I don't know whether you would agree, Mr. Krajisnik, of course, I had not the help of any numbers added to it and I'm -- I could find it most of the time but never on the page you indicated. So there might be a problem there as well. But perhaps you pay some attention to it, and, of course, I used the electronic version where the page numbering is at the top of the page and where the last page of this document, let me just compare perhaps the ERN numbers, page 61 bears ERN number 00898123.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I explain to you? Very often there is a double recording of assemblies. For example, I have here SA 000. Then I have two footnotes. This other version. So you probably have another version. I managed to find every page here in Mr. Stewart's document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, does the ERN number --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't coincide, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again we are working. I was focusing now on the tab 88, which is -- let me just have a look. I think it's 64 A, tab 88 but it could be P65 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the reference -- it's just a note, Your Honour, was P65, binder 8, tab 88.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I used that one but the one that is it stored by the Registrar and I noticed that there must be different versions of that document in the original as well because sometimes I see some differences in the headings, in the B/C/S version and the translation. So there again, I'm very much concerned, although most of it is -- seems to be exactly -- seems to be the same but we should be aware to avoid to at all costs to work from different versions of the same documents, whether different versions in B/C/S or different versions in the translation. I just have drawn attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely in principle I completely agree, Your Honour. The explanation as far as this item is concerned is that they are not two different translations. One is a -- as I understand it, one is a stenographic recording of the session and the other is a tape recording. So they are actually -- they are two different Serbian records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, when I asked your attention for the ERN numbers and they are different, and it's clear already that there are two B/C/S versions as well. So therefore -- but I don't think it's dramatic at this moment but especially since you're going into quite some detail I'm a bit concerned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, in this particular case as well, I believe it's correct to say that if there is a value judgement to be made the tape recorded version is actually better than the stenographic one, but that may be a personal view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it seems that the one which -- the tape is better than the stenographic one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It seems to be, without my being able to check against the original Serbian, Your Honour, but it seems to be fuller in some way which is perhaps not -- I don't want to offend any stenographer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's mainly that the parties should be aware to rely as good as they can on the documents as stored by the Registry and they can be found on the judicial database, almost all of them. If not I'm certain that Mr. Registrar will help you, as he does now and then, if one of the documents is not found he sends it to me by e-mail as an attachment and I can open it immediately. So there are always ways of using the documents as admitted, which I very much prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May I say this? First of all we do very much appreciate that help which is continuing and considerable and we do take full advantage of it, Your Honour. A point I would 100 per cent acknowledge is that we owe it to Your Honours to alert you whenever there are two different versions and Your Honours may be inconvenienced in that way. But I will also add this, Your Honour, that 23 if the Prosecution have chosen to exhibit, and the Trial Chamber, to exhibit a particular version of a document, and we, the Defence, do for good reason consider that a different version is preferable, then, well, Your Honour, that is a request we would reserve the right to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is no way of -- that the Chamber would -- the Chamber is just concerned about the possible confusion, not about one party suggesting that a better translation or a better original would be used. I mean, the best is not even good enough for us, but I just establish that both in translation and in the originals and for the translation certainly the -- I have to look at the Prosecution, where it seems that many documents have been translated more than once, that we should avoid that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Defence says yes to all that, Your Honour, with respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was just on my feet for one small, practical suggestion. I think we are bringing in anticipation of moving ahead to in a chronological manner to other sessions, copies of those sessions we have attempted it in so far as possible to match those to what we understand to be actual exhibits. So if Mr. Stewart will simply identify the ERN of the B/C/S version as well as the interpretation he has, we can check those immediately against the copies we brought. Again, I can't ensure with 100 per cent accuracy that they do represent the actual documents in evidence but we have attempted to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to do that during the Court hearings but, of course, it's better done prior to that. I'm also concerned not only about the Chamber being confused by the witness and the accused, the present witness and the accused, could be confused by this as well because he answers questions on the basis of his B/C/S original usually and he might not be aware that a question is phrased in accordance with either a different original and its translation or one of the two versions of the translation. So therefore, it's -- I'm just asking and insisting on greatest precision by the parties. Let's not spend more time on it unless there is really something very important. Let's try to clarify these issues before court and not during the testimony, and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ten seconds' practical matter. Mr. Sladojevic can answer all inquiries on these matters of ERN numbers and so on and I'm sure would be happy to send an e-mail listing what we are coming to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, even if he's not happy I'm sort of saying he should.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a new style of management. If you're not happy, you should. I'll keep that in mind for my staff, Mr. Stewart. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't quite say that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, there is an exhibit that I -- may not give rise to specific questions but nevertheless --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, a useful thing to have a look at. It's P211. We did notify that this might be an exhibit we would refer to. Your Honour, I mention it because -- well, first of all it's rather a long time, that's not a good reason in itself but it's rather a long timing since we looked at this map. It was produced during the evidence of Mr. Okun, a long time ago, and among other things, it was before Judge Hanoteau joined the case so he didn't have the pleasure of looking at this map when it was originally produced. I wouldn't know among the many, many exhibits in this case how much opportunity has been taken for familiarisation with it but it's -- it is a -- it's based on the 1991 census and it appears from its date, Your Honour, it's -- it seems to be produced around August 1991. And from the legend -- it's all in Serbian, Your Honour, but from the legend on the left, the colouring it's not quite the colouring that matches what Mr. Krajisnik said yesterday. It's blue for Croats, green for Muslims and then a -- I don't know what you would call it it's a sort of orangey colour for Serbs, and then yellow for Yugoslavs. And the -- where it shows majority, it also ties in with the observation Your Honour made a few moments ago about the question relating to variants A and B, that if we take, for example, the Croat municipalities in blue, where they got more than 66 per cent of the population, it's a solid, dark blue, where they've got between 50 and 66 per cent it's a lighter blue, and then it's the white-hatched blue where there is the relative majority that Your Honour was asking about in that context a few minutes ago. And then very helpfully, the percentages of the population of the other ethnic groups are given in the sort of mini bar chart in the middle of the municipalities. So this is the 1991 census. It's a pretty good map, if I may say so, simply didn't produce it myself, from the point of view of information because it also gives on the right a picture of the position in 1971 and then it gives various other information relating to 1981 to 1991 movements, and then in the bottom right, because Sarajevo obviously can't be easily fitted into a map of this scale, Sarajevo is taken out separately as a block. So the Sarajevo municipalities are shown. But the reason I raise it at that this point, Your Honour, is not because it gives rise to any questions but it does appear to the Defence now to be revived as a useful map to have in mind when we are considering such matters as Cutileiro and so on and when we are looking at some of the remaining elements of the case. And it's terribly easy for anybody involved in this case to forget about a map like this two years later. It's lurking there among the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It certainly will assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, have not actually -- you haven't actually got it in front of you, I think, but if I perhaps if I just hand it to Mr. Krajisnik and he can confirm --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it a map that you've seen it in the course -- oh, yes it's up on the screen. You've seen it in the course of this case, Mr. Krajisnik, but is it a map that you had available to you and did look at in the course of late 1991, early 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This map or a similar map we saw at the time. However, I have to draw your attention to something else, that it was not the subject, if I can put it that way, of our discussions with Mr. Cutileiro because this is a map of municipalities. It is not a land registry map. I have a map here of Bosnia-Herzegovina that is based on the land registry and that was presented here and I can explain why it is not convenient for the establishment of constituent units but I am familiar with this map. I know this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, before we come on to more specific questions about that, the -- one of the features of the map that we are looking at right now, P211, useful though it might be, is that it just deals with it municipality by municipality, doesn't it, so that the smallest block for which we see information on this map is a municipality. That's perhaps to a considerable extent the point you were making a moment ago, is it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You're quite right. You can see here which municipality has a majority and which could become part of the region, those that don't have it could not, because they haven't got that particular type of population or a majority in the municipality. It's interesting for clarifying variants A and B who was a majority and who was a minority. However, for Cutileiro plan you need a different map where in the municipalities you can see which local communities are minority ones and which are majority ones. We can now look at all of Bosnia-Herzegovina as 43 per cent, so it all looks yellow or blue or -- you're quite right. You should really look at municipalities in their entirety and what the percentage of the population is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just by way of groundwork again, you've made a reference a moment ago to a map you have with you here. Again, by here, you mean not in this courtroom with you today, but here with you in The Hague, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I mean here in my bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might just because it can only help to resolve any possible misunderstanding, it might be helpful if Mr. Krajisnik could be permitted to produce that map and then we can make sure overnight perhaps that it's -- it matches what we've got and isn't going to cause any confusion in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you, Mr. Stewart, whether you would invite Mr. Krajisnik. I mean we have heard evidence several times that in terms of lands ownership that quite a few municipalities would be majority Serb where the population would not -- of course, the next question is whether the -- whether decisions are taken by land owners or by citizens. I mean, even if we would accept, and I think it's not contested until now, Mr. Harmon, that the -- some municipalities would have over 50 per cent of land owned by Serbs, whether that would be a legitimate ground for claims or whether population percentages would be a legitimate ground for claims is, of course, a matter still to be seen but there seems to be not that much of a difference. At least I've never heard any cross-examination on disputing that landownership might have been quite different and more favourable to the Serbs than the composition of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's not completely consistent with my recollection, Your Honour. I do recall evidence during the course of the Prosecution case that a great deal of land was state-owned and that the claim of landownership, particularly the 64 per cent claim that was, as Mr. Krajisnik indicated today, was bandied about considerably, was inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now do remember that there was some dispute about to what extent the claim of landownership was justified especially in relation to land which was not privately owned. I apologise for not having remembered that but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave it to you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That came up specifically in the evidence of Mr. Okun; wherever it came up, it certainly came up in the course of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I misstated it at this moment but sometimes I have to -- I was not prepared for this issue at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Like the maps, Your Honour, some of the evidence was a long time ago as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I leave it up to you whether you find it of such importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd like the map, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't do any harm just to check that it's something new --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you're invited to provide the map you have with you to Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can tell Your Honour I have no enthusiasm for one more map unless it is strictly relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a map of Sarajevo here and a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But there is not a Serb map. It is a map of an official authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so these percentages are completely different. This map was already exhibited here. This is Sarajevo. This is Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour it was really just to confirm this. I think I can see from here although they are quite detailed, that they are maps already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If they are exhibited, there is no need to -- then most important us is to find out under what numbers. Yes, I certainly remember this -- these ones. Perhaps they are two that are the same. I certainly remember the blue and rose one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour would the most helpful thing be perhaps if Mr. Krajisnik can bear to part with them over night we will take them, and double check that they are the same as what's been exhibited, and get it all sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, based upon our quick glance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see at this moment -- we have P68, in which at least the blue and rose map appears.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's an exhibit with a number of different tabs, isn't it, Your Honour, from Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The one I'm referring to is tab 2. I could just briefly check on whether ---

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe it's also P293.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P293. Yes so that's already exhibited twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Too much to hope it's only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To restore the equality of arms you're entitled to exhibit it twice as well, Mr. Stewart. I'm just looking at whether the third map, the blue and green one, is already here in this bundle. I think as a matter of fact it is not. I think it's not. If you would pay specific attention to the blue and green overnight, the other two are exhibited, Mr. Krajisnik, so they could be returned to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. May we do that, then, Your Honour? We'll pass them to our cartographical assistant, through Mr. Josse to our cartographical assistant, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I would wish to you have at this point D5 and D6. They go in reverse chronological order. D6 comes first. Now, does D6 appear to you to be what is commonly known as the Lisbon Agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Lisbon Agreement is both the Lisbon agreement and the Sarajevo agreement. So it's two agreements. And two statements of principles have been attached here. What I got here is the first variant that was agreed in Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's a statement of principles and it -- to identify it, it begins as well as being marked D6. I hope that Bosnia and Herzegovina would, after independence, be an independent state composed of three constituent and then it's got in square brackets, unit, named ... and then there is an asterisk indicating the word for these constituent units requires further consideration.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker slow down the interpreters did not receive the text. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, a bit fast. The constituent, in brackets, units, and then there is a asterisk against that and at the bottom, asterisk, the word for these constituent units requires further consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This document, the original of this document was not in your language, was it, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time, not when we talked. It was translated quickly because it was short. Perhaps during the course of the same day or the following day, I was aware of the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the -- is it correct the -- the meetings at which this document emerged was held in Lisbon just a few days after the assembly session that we were considering a few minutes ago, the 15th of February 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But as far as I can remember, the date on this document was the 13th of March. But it can be checked in the original. So after the 25th of February, this meeting in Lisbon took place. I think it was the 13th of March. And the second one on the 18th of March, as far as I can remember. It can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well any way there was a gap -- there was a gap between the two, wasn't there, when the talks were adjourned or suspended -- no, not suspended, the talks were adjourned and everybody returned home and then you resumed, didn't you, after that gap? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if you can be given D5, if you don't already have it, and that's -- but, of course, here you're disadvantaged here, Mr. Krajisnik, by the fact that you are looking at the document that is in English but it bears a date at the end, Sarajevo, 18th March 1992. And that's consistent with, is it, with your recollection that it was at that time in March that the second version emerged?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the version after the Sarajevo meeting. You're right. This is the second version, the amended and final one, final as it was at the time, that all three parties stated their views on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Krajisnik, that -- that -- there never did purport to be final, confirmed agreement of either of these documents by the parties to those discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Defence please move the microphone away from the -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you explain that a bit? I don't quite understand final. This was sort of the final document that we agreed on but it had not been elaborated. That is to say that what was envisaged was that a complete plan should be made now and then perhaps signed, if I understood this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I was asking, I'll put it in neutral terms, was it -- was it -- were either of these documents agreed as a binding agreement among the parties?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These principles were agreed on as binding, but if I understand your question, we called this the Lisbon Agreement but on the basis of these principles, we did not make a complete plan like the Owen-Stoltenberg plan or the Dayton plan ultimately that was signed as such and that was binding. But all four parties, that is to say the European Community and the three parties, accepted these principles. So then it is a well known thing what the experts are supposed to do to make maps and work on this and so on and so forth. So actually the only real question that we were discussing all the time and where we had disagreements, if I can put it that way, was the map. Everything else was easier to agree upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, there is a D7A and a D7B; Mr. Krajisnik, I don't think you have those yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see a D7 and a D7A. I take it that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D7 being one with some handwritten text at the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour I had it marked as D7A but if that's D7, may I ask Your Honour, are they technically what? 7 and 7A? Just so I know for future reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. D7 is the I would say the more or less handwritten, where the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the other one is D7 B which doesn't make that much sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's perfect, Your Honour. Could Mr. Krajisnik have those?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you see, there are two different maps. Mr. Krajisnik, do you recognise either or both of those?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise both.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We either need a copy of D7 A or need it put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can put it on the ELMO. That's being done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way of copying the whole list of exhibits? I can find it on my computer within a second approximately. It's just a matter of copying the complete set of exhibits as we have it on the computer so that you could just find it immediately, Mr. Tieger. I'm not saying that you're not entitled to have a hard copy in your hands but very often it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we believe that's still at this point in the case technically or practically not quite achievable or not achievable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would surprise me. It seems to be such an easy thing to just to have the scanned exhibits which are --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not everything has been scanned, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A lot has been scanned by now, it's almost complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not quibbling about it. A lot has been scanned but given the scale, a lot hasn't been scanned because the -- Mr. Treanor's stuff, for example, is thousands of pages. That's the problem Your Honour. Your Honour is absolutely right. A great deal has been scanned. A great deal hasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would say a great majority has been scanned by now. It's not really complete but it's -- even the Treanor Exhibit 64 A, 65, is -- it's almost complete and we'll find a way of accommodating you because I'm very concerned about having to print out everything again and again and it saves a lot of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we acknowledge great progress has been made recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are where we are. And that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I would say, Your Honour, is obviously it's tremendously helpful if whatever anybody -- because this is neutral, after all, whatever anybody has everybody else should have. But that can be sorted out behind the scenes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Krajisnik, what is this that you're seeing on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see on the screen is the Cutileiro map as it was proposed to us in Sarajevo at that last meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the other map, then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The other map -- well, these two maps were published in the newspapers too. This other map is the proposal of the Muslim side and that created confusion. Before the Cutileiro map, all three parties had given their proposals to Mr. Cutileiro, so this was the proposal of the Muslim side. All three maps were published here as well as the Cutileiro map. I think that that has even been exhibited already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, probably, Mr. Krajisnik. So the position is very clear, is it, that the -- the first of those maps we looked at, which is 7 B, I think, the one with the -- the horizontal hatching across it, that was actually part of the agreement, that was attached to the agreement. The other one, the Muslim map you referred to, wasn't. That was one of a number of maps which were put forward and had been under discussion? Is that a correct summary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJSINIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. Just a small correction: This map of Cutileiro's was a working map. They said, well, this is the map we propose along with this agreement, and on this map it says that we are going to establish teams that are going to make some smaller territorial corrections or whatever, and that we'll accommodate their views. You saw in the principles of the 13th of March that it said according to the census of 1971, 1981, and 1991 respectively. This was aimed at making a map that would be as accurate as possible. The Croatian side asked for the census of 1971, we asked for the census of 1981, and the Muslim side asked for the census of 1991. So more work had to be done but the working map that we had all agreed on in a preliminary way, I cannot say was a final one because it still needed additional work to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it be convenient to pause there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It is, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Krajisnik, even if I would not remind you that you should not speak to anyone about your testimony already given or still to be given, you would accept that anyhow, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have frightened me so much that I don't dare say a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the interpreters are frightened by the Prosecution. Let's not discuss the matter. So therefore, since you understand it, there is no need to remind you of it. We will adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume tomorrow morning, 9.00, in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
